newsitem.title: USA: House votes to keep timber road subsidies.
newsitem.headline: House votes to keep timber road subsidies.

text.p: The House defeated Thursday an effort to halt subsidies to timber companies that build logging roads in national forests.

Instead, the House passed a compromise that modestly trims the program that timber companies say is essential to keep them operating in many areas. But environmentalists say the road-building program amounts to a subsidy to loggers for wreaking environmental havoc.

The House voted 211 to 209 for the compromise that would cut $5.6 million from U.S. Forest Service spending on new roads, and would scale back a program in which the Forest Service offers trees to logging companies in exchange for building roads.
Democrats and some eastern Republicans pushed a stiffer measure that would have cut $41.5 million from road building and halted the payment-in-kind program for new roads.

"Enough is enough. We don't need any new taxpayer subsidized logging roads," said Massachusetts Democratic Rep. Joseph Kennedy, who sponsored the measure to halt subsidies along with Illinois Republican Rep. John Edward Porter.
Their measure would have cut funds to build some 300 miles of new roads and rebuild some 2,000 miles next year.
But Washington Democratic Rep. Norman Dicks, who pushed the compromise, said their bill would have harmed the timber industry and many rural communities.

"Timber sales are down from around 12 billion board feet in the '80s to 3.7 billion board feet. If we're going to have access even to the 3.7 billion board feet we've got to have some additional new roads," he said.

Dicks and other timber state lawmakers said timber roads in national forests -- which are a denser network than on non-forest land -- also are essential byways for recreation, access to isolated communities and for fighting fires.
"You go in on road to fight the fire, you go in on a road for recreation, and yes, you go in on a road to take out timber," West Virginia Democratic Rep. Robert Wise said.
But environmentalists say the 378,000 miles of logging roads that crisscross national forests cause mudslides, wash into streams and kill fish, change drainage patterns, and damage wildlife habitat.

"The construction of the logging roads, and once they are in place, is one of the more destructive activities the Forest Service undertakes. They erode, and when the road fails, everything goes down the hill," Marty Hayden, senior policy analyst with the Earthjustic Legal Defense Fund, said.
Hayden said the Kennedy-Porter amendment failed because "the Forest Service and USDA (U.S. Agriculture Department) pulled out all the stops for the timber industry."

Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman, who oversees the Forest Service, in a letter said small timber companies would be hurt if the trees-for-roads program were eliminated, and said the Kennedy-Porter plan went "too far in eliminating important construction and reconstruction efforts that provide public safety and environmental benefits."
